concepts.def: Analysing an anthropological text by identifying its argument, examining its evidence and assessing how persuasively its conclusions are supported.
The central claim an author makes about a society, which students must locate, summarise and evaluate when engaging critically with material.
The fieldwork data, observations and examples an anthropologist uses to support claims, which readers should assess for relevance and sufficiency.
A focused question that guides the internal assessment, directing the student to interrogate a specific aspect of an anthropological source.
The set of concepts and perspectives an anthropologist uses to interpret data, which shapes their conclusions and can itself be evaluated.
Judging the strengths and limitations of an anthropological account, considering bias, context, method and the persuasiveness of its reasoning.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Internal Assessment: Critical Engagement — a core area of Social and Cultural Anthropology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Internal Assessment: Critical Engagement brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Internal Assessment: Critical Engagement.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Critically engaging with an anthropological source begins with:
options: Identifying the author's central argument
Counting the number of pages
Copying it out word for word
Ignoring the evidence given

mcqs.q: Evaluating the 'evidence base' of an ethnography means assessing:
options: Whether the data supports the claims
The design of the book cover
The age of the author
The font that was used
Focus critical analysis on a specific aspect of the source
Summarise the whole of anthropology
Decorate the title page
Avoid doing any analysis

mcqs.q: A strong critical engagement considers an account's:
options: Strengths and limitations
Strengths only
Length only
Price only

mcqs.q: What is the first step in critically engaging with an anthropological source?
options: Praising it without any analysis.
Counting the number of references.
Identifying the author's central argument.
Agreeing with the source before reading it fully.

mcqs.q: What does evaluating the 'evidence base' involve?
options: Measuring the length of the text.
Judging whether the fieldwork data adequately supports the claims.
Praising it without any analysis.
Checking only whether the writing is enjoyable.

mcqs.q: What makes a critical engagement balanced?
options: Considering both the strengths and the limitations of the account.
Measuring the length of the text.
Praising it without any analysis.
Listing only its weaknesses.
